lesson.title: Dissolve or Not? A Practical Guide to Solubility Rules
lesson.summary: Solubility rules are a set of empirically derived guidelines that let you predict, without running the experiment, whether an ionic compound will dissolve in water or remain a solid.
lesson.body:
Solubility introduced the general idea that how much of a substance dissolves in a solvent depends on a competition between the forces holding the solid together and the forces the solvent can offer instead. Ionic Compounds taught you that ionic solids are held together by strong electrostatic attractions between cations and anions arranged in a lattice. Put those two ideas together for an ionic compound in water, and dissolving becomes a contest between the lattice energy holding the ions together and the hydration energy released when water molecules surround and stabilize the separated ions. Calculating both of those energies precisely is genuinely difficult, so rather than doing that math every time, chemists rely on a set of solubility rules distilled from decades of experimental observation.

The rules that matter most for general and AP chemistry are these. Compounds of Group 1 metals, Li+, Na+, K+, Rb+, Cs+, and of the ammonium ion, NH4+, are essentially always soluble, with no exceptions worth memorizing. Nitrates, NO3-, acetates, CH3COO-, and chlorates, ClO3-, are essentially always soluble as well. Most chlorides, bromides, and iodides are soluble, except when paired with silver, Ag+, lead(II), Pb2+, or mercury(I), Hg2^2+, which form insoluble halides. Most sulfates are soluble, except with barium, Ba2+, strontium, Sr2+, and lead(II), Pb2+, and calcium sulfate is only slightly soluble. Most hydroxides are insoluble, except those of Group 1 metals and the more soluble Ba(OH)2 and Sr(OH)2, with Ca(OH)2 falling in between as only slightly soluble. Finally, most carbonates, phosphates, sulfides, and chromates are insoluble, except when paired with Group 1 metals or ammonium.

Notice the pattern behind the exceptions: it is almost always Group 1 metals and ammonium on the soluble side, and it is almost always the same handful of cations, silver, lead, barium, strontium, showing up as the exceptions on the insoluble side. Rather than treating this as an arbitrary list to memorize word for word, it helps to remember the short list of always soluble cations and anions first, then learn the handful of documented exceptions that reverse the usual pattern.

You can use these rules to predict what will happen before you mix two solutions. Suppose you combine aqueous lead(II) nitrate with aqueous potassium iodide. The possible new pairings, after a double replacement swap, are PbI2 and KNO3. Checking the rules: KNO3 pairs a Group 1 cation with nitrate, both always soluble categories, so it stays fully dissolved. PbI2 pairs iodide with lead(II), exactly one of the documented halide exceptions, so it is insoluble. The prediction is that a solid, PbI2, should separate out of the mixture. As it happens, that is a real and visually striking reaction, bright yellow lead(II) iodide crystals forming almost instantly, and it is exactly the reaction the next chapter examines in detail.
